text:
Maya Lin: Heads up — noticed a weird routing surge on the canary for /v1/generate. Canary is 5% but one canary pool got ~40% of traffic for a few minutes starting 12:02 UTC. Dashboard shows big latency bump. Anyone seen this pattern before?
Carl D: Ugh. Any correlation with header-based routing or experiments?
Maya Lin: Looks like a subset of requests had no session cookie (cookie churn from mobile clients). We use header override X-Exp to force canary for some A/B tests. Seems when cookie is missing, header wins but our sticky hashing then pushes many of those into a single canary host bucket.
Jen S: Can you paste the route config? I'm guessing evaluation order is header -> stickiness -> hash. If header is evaluated before cookie-stickiness we can bias distribution when cookie absent.
Maya Lin: Here is the simplified rule from the console (sanitized):
```yaml
route: /v1/generate
- guard: header X-Exp == "canary" -> route: canary
- guard: cookie session_id -> sticky: session_id -> weighted_split: canary:5, primary:95
- fallback: consistent_hash(client_ip)
```
Tash: That ordering explains it. If many clients have no cookie but X-Exp present, they all hit header path and then fallback consistent_hash buckets can be skewed because of low cardinality (mobile NAT).
Kev: Telemetry corroborates — one canary host shows 70% of the canary requests in that window. Host affinity + NATted IPs.
ops-bot: deploy-bot noticed a canary rollout started at 11:58 UTC (release/2026-02-18-canary).
deploy-bot: CI deployment passed, canary=5% applied to route=/v1/generate.
Carl D: Short term mitigation: flip header override to only apply for requests with a session cookie, or temporarily disable header override while we patch route evaluation.
Jen S: Agreed. Also add a guard that requires cookie OR header + random-sample to avoid cluster bias. Something like: header X-Exp==canary AND rand() < 0.05 when cookie absent.
Maya Lin: Can someone apply a quick rollback to header policy? I don't want to roll the whole canary back if we can limit the header path.
Kev: I pushed a conservative change to the edge feature flag: route.guard.header_override_enabled -> false for /v1/generate (rolled at 12:10 UTC). Confirmed drop in skew by 12:14 UTC.
Tash: Recorded the incident in the console: created a new telemetry panel for "route: canary header_override hits" and added an alert threshold at 10% of canary traffic per host.
Carl D: Follow-ups: (1) change evaluation order to check cookie stickiness before header override; (2) add sampling gate for header-only hits; (3) update runbook and console UX to make header overrides explicit with a warning about low-cardinality sources.
Jen S: I'll open a PR with the route engine change — should be a small patch in route-evaluator to reorder checks and add the sampling helper.
Maya Lin: Thanks — once PR is up, can we do a quick canary of the route-evaluator change itself on a low-traffic route first? Prefer not to surprise /v1/generate again.
Kev: Yep. I also dumped request logs for 12:00-12:15 to S3: s3://redwood-debug/route-spike/1781234567.log (redacted). Contains client_ip distribution and X-Exp headers.
Tash: Putting this on retro agenda: make routing rules ordering and sticky behavior visible in the console UI. Right now it's too easy to add a header rule that bypasses stickiness. :white_flag:
Maya Lin: TL;DR — header override + missing cookies + NATted IPs = hash bucket bias. Temporary fix applied (disabled header override), follow-ups listed. Thanks all.
Kev: Adding a short postmortem note in #postmortems after Jen's PR lands.
Jen S: PR: github.com/redwood/route-eval/pull/842 (draft) — includes unit test for cookie-first ordering and a sampling helper.
Carl D: Nice. Once tests pass, let's schedule the low-traffic canary tomorrow morning.
Maya Lin: Closing the thread — monitoring green, will re-open if we see recurrence. :thumbsup:
